title: I. Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a landowner well known in our district in his day, and still remembered here because of his gloomy and violent death, which happened thirteen years ago, and which I'll describe in its proper place. For now I'll only say that this “landowner”—as we used to call him, though he barely spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange sort, yet one you run into fairly often: abject and vicious, and at the same time senseless. But he was one of those senseless men who are perfectly capable of managing their worldly affairs, and, it seemed, of nothing else. Fyodor Pavlovitch, for instance, started out with next to nothing; his estate was tiny; he ran around dining at other men's tables, sponging off them like a hanger-on, and yet by the time he died it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in cash. And all the while he remained one of the most senseless, fantastical men in the whole district. I repeat, it wasn't stupidity—most of these fantastical men are shrewd and intelligent enough—it was simply senselessness, a peculiar, homegrown kind of it.

He was married twice, and had three sons: the eldest, Dmitri, by his first wife, and two more, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, came from a fairly rich and distinguished noble family, also landowners in our district—the Miüsovs. How it happened that an heiress, and a beauty besides, one of those vigorous, intelligent girls so common in this generation but sometimes found in the last one too, could have married such a worthless, puny weakling as we all called him, I won't try to explain. I once knew a young lady of that last “romantic” generation who, after years of a mysterious passion for a man she could easily have married at any moment, invented insurmountable obstacles to their union and ended by throwing herself, on a stormy night, into a rather deep, fast river from a high bank—almost a cliff—and perished there, purely to satisfy her own whim, to be like Shakespeare's Ophelia. In fact, if that cliff, her favorite chosen spot, had been less picturesque—if there had been an ordinary flat bank there instead—the suicide probably would never have happened. That's a fact, and there have surely been more than a few similar cases in the last two or three generations. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov's action was, no doubt, likewise an echo of other people's ideas, brought on by the irritation of having no mental freedom of her own. She wanted, perhaps, to show her independence as a woman, to rise above class distinctions and her family's tyranny. And a pliable imagination convinced her, we must suppose, for one brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, despite his parasitic standing, was one of the bold, ironic spirits of that progressive age—when in fact he was nothing but an ill-natured buffoon. What gave the marriage its spice was that it was preceded by an elopement, and this captivated Adelaïda Ivanovna's imagination completely. Fyodor Pavlovitch's position at the time made him especially eager for any such venture, since he was desperate to make a career for himself one way or another. Attaching himself to a good family and getting a dowry was an alluring prospect. As for mutual love, there was apparently none of it, not on the bride's side and not on his, despite Adelaïda Ivanovna's beauty. This was, perhaps, a unique case in the life of Fyodor Pavlovitch, a man of an always lustful temperament, ready to chase after any skirt at the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the one woman who made no particular appeal to his senses.

Immediately after the elopement Adelaïda Ivanovna realized in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. The marriage showed its true colors with extraordinary speed. Although her family accepted the affair fairly quickly and settled her dowry on the runaway bride, husband and wife began leading a thoroughly disorderly life, and there were endless scenes between them. It was said that the young wife showed far more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch, who, as we now know, got hold of all her money—up to twenty-five thousand roubles—the moment she received it, so that sum was lost to her forever. The little village and the rather fine town house that made up the rest of her dowry he did his utmost, for a long time, to transfer into his own name by means of some deed of conveyance. He probably would have succeeded, simply from her moral exhaustion and her desire to be rid of him, and from the contempt and disgust his persistent, shameless pestering aroused in her. But luckily Adelaïda Ivanovna's family stepped in and blocked his greed. It's known for a fact that there were frequent fights between husband and wife, but rumor had it that Fyodor Pavlovitch did not beat his wife, but was beaten by her, since she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman of remarkable physical strength. In the end she left the house and ran off from Fyodor Pavlovitch with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a three-year-old, in her husband's hands. Fyodor Pavlovitch promptly installed a regular harem in the house and gave himself over to drunken orgies. In the intervals he would drive all over the province, weeping to everyone about Adelaïda Ivanovna having left him, going into details too shameful for a husband to mention about his own married life. What seemed to please him most, flattering his vanity, was playing the ridiculous role of the wronged husband and parading his sorrows with embellishments.

“Anyone would think you'd gotten a promotion, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you seem so pleased despite your grief,” mockers said to him. Many even added that he was glad of a new comic role in which to play the buffoon, and that it was precisely to make it funnier that he pretended not to notice his ridiculous position. But who knows—it may just have been simplicity. At last he managed to track down his runaway wife. The poor woman turned out to be in Petersburg, where she had gone with her divinity student and had thrown herself into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once began bustling about, making preparations to go to Petersburg—for what purpose he couldn't have said himself. He probably would have actually gone; but having decided to go, he felt entitled at once to fortify himself for the trip with another bout of reckless drinking. And it was just then that his wife's family received news of her death in Petersburg. She had died suddenly, in a garret—of typhus, according to one story, or, as another version had it, of starvation. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife's death, and the story goes that he ran out into the street and began shouting for joy, raising his hands to heaven: “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace,” though others say he wept without restraint, like a small child, so much so that people felt sorry for him despite the revulsion he inspired. It's entirely possible both versions were true—that he rejoiced at his release and at the same time wept for the woman who had released him. As a rule, people, even wicked ones, are far more naive and simple-hearted than we assume. And so are we ourselves, for that matter.
